column3: This is Worksight. Visual inspection that learns from good parts only.
A new part arrives on the line. Defects are rare, maybe one in a thousand.
A typical model needs hundreds of labelled defects, and weeks of labelling. And every new part starts again.
What if you only needed good photos?
Worksight takes twenty photos of good parts and builds a profile in about nine seconds. No defect labels. No training run.
Here is how it works. A frozen ResNet-18 turns every patch of the photo into a feature vector.
Each patch is matched to its nearest good patch from the profile.
The distance becomes a heatmap and an anomaly score. Above the threshold, the part fails.
And it does this for every board, in about a third of a second on a CPU. Only the anomalies reach the engineer.

Then Gemma, running on AMD GPUs through AMD Token Factory, looks at the photo, the heatmap, the closest good reference and the part's documents. It explains in plain words what looks wrong and what to check first.
It explains. It never changes the decision.
Everything lives on one screen: the heatmap, the closest reference, pass, fail or needs review, Gemma's explanation and a one-page report.
With history, batch inspection and seven interface languages.
And the engineer always decides. The model's decision and the engineer's decision are stored separately.

On four circuit-board sets from the public VisA dataset, AUROC ranges from 0.875 to 0.992. Counting the review band, fifty-six to ninety-six percent of defects reach the engineer. Every number is measured on a held-out test.
Seventy-four commits, eighty-one automated tests, built in two days, and fully open source.
PyTorch, FastAPI and Next.js, with Gemma on AMD Token Factory, deployed on Railway.
No expensive inspection rig: just a camera and a CPU server.
And defects are caught on the line, before they ship, so there are fewer returns and compensation claims.
Worksight, by Desert Eagles. Try it at the link on screen.
